numerical_failure.observed_behavior: On non-nanosecond datetime-like data, `round`/`floor`/`ceil` with an incompatible `freq` silently rounds to the wrong granularity. Example: `pd.Timedelta("6s").as_unit("s").round("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:06')` (i.e., 6s instead of 5s). Example: `pd.Timedelta("4s").as_unit("s").ceil("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:04')`, which is not a multiple of the requested `freq` at all.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: Correct behavior is to classify `freq` against one unit of the target resolution: (1) if `freq` is a whole multiple of the unit, round normally; (2) if `freq` divides one unit evenly, it is a no-op; otherwise raise `ValueError` using the message already raised in `core/arrays/_ranges.py` for this exact situation (including `freq="2500ms"` on second-resolution data).
trigger_conditions: Calling `round`/`floor`/`ceil` with a `freq` on non-nanosecond datetime-like data (i.e., when object resolution is not nanosecond).

`freq` is not exactly representable at the object's resolution; prior behavior used `get_unit_for_round(..., round_ok=True)` which silently truncated `freq` and rounded to a different granularity than requested.
Specifically reproduced when using second-resolution data (`.as_unit("s")`) with `freq="2500ms"`.
This reproduces for `Timestamp`, `DatetimeIndex`, `TimedeltaIndex`, and `Series.dt` because all call sites share the helper.

Datapath: `get_unit_for_round` uses `convert_reso(..., round_ok=False)` and checks `td._value % factor != 0` to decide incompatibility; otherwise it returns a `no-op` indicator (`0`) when `factor % td._value == 0`.

oracle_clues: PR body states: `Timedelta("6s").as_unit("s").round("2500ms")` should be `5s` (but the provided passages show only the buggy return value).
PR body states `.ceil("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:04')`, which is “not a multiple of the requested freq at all”; it should instead raise `ValueError` for incompatible `freq`.

The fix description says incompatible `freq` now raises `ValueError`, reusing the message from `core/arrays/_ranges.py` for this exact situation (`s.resample("2500ms")` on second-resolution data is cited).

Tests (described in the provided evidence) expect `pytest.raises(ValueError, match=rf"freq=.* is incompatible with unit={unit}")` when `freq` is neither a multiple nor divisor (e.g., for `DatetimeIndex` with `(unit,freq)` pairs (`s`,`700ms`), (`s`,`2500ms`), (`ms`,`3us`), (`us`,`300ns`)).

category_specific_evidence: Violated mathematical/representability property: for rounding methods (round/floor/ceil), the requested `freq` must be compatible with the index/scalar unit resolution such that the rounded result would be representable; equivalently, `freq` must be classified as either (1) a whole multiple of one unit of the target resolution (rounds normally), (2) a divisor of one unit that divides evenly (no-op because every representable value is already a multiple), or (3) otherwise incompatible and must raise `ValueError`.

Concrete failing values demonstrating the violation (old behavior): `Timedelta("6s").as_unit("s").round("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:06')` instead of `5s` (as described in the passage: “instead of 5s”).

Concrete failing values demonstrating the violation (old behavior): `Timedelta("4s").as_unit("s").ceil("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:04')`, and this is “not a multiple of the requested freq at all.”

New required behavior evidenced by tests: for `DatetimeIndex`, with `dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(["2020-01-01 00:00:06.500000001"])`, each of `method in ["round","floor","ceil"]` must raise `ValueError` when `freq` is neither a multiple nor a divisor of one unit of the resolution, with parametrized pairs: (`unit`,`freq`) = (`s`,`700ms`), (`s`,`2500ms`), (`ms`,`3us`), (`us`,`300ns`).

Test assertion about incompatibility message: `msg = rf"freq=.* is incompatible with unit={unit}"` and the code expects `pytest.raises(ValueError, match=msg)` for `getattr(dti.as_unit(unit), method)(freq)` (and similarly for `Timestamp` and `Timedelta`).
reproduction_risks: Reproduction may fail if the chosen input value lies on the `freq` grid such that rounding becomes a no-op; the passages emphasize using values “deliberately off the freq grid” (e.g., `"2020-01-01 00:00:06.500000001"` or `Timedelta("6.500000001s")`) so the incorrect-granularity behavior is observable (old truncation could otherwise appear as a no-op).

provenance.value: On non-nanosecond data, round/floor/ceil silently rounded to an incorrect granularity when the requested `freq` was neither a whole multiple of the object's resolution nor an exact divisor. Examples: `pd.Timedelta("6s").as_unit("s").round("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:06')` and `pd.Timedelta("4s").as_unit("s").ceil("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:04')` (the latter is not a multiple of the requested freq).

Instead of rounding to the wrong frequency, the operation should either (a) round normally when `freq` is a whole multiple of the unit at the target resolution, (b) be a no-op when `freq` divides one unit evenly, or (c) raise `ValueError` when `freq` is incompatible with the target unit (including the demonstrated case `freq="2500ms"` on second-resolution data), using the message already raised in `core/arrays/_ranges.py` for this exact situation.

On non-nanosecond datetime-like data, `round`/`floor`/`ceil` with an incompatible `freq` silently rounds to the wrong granularity. Example: `pd.Timedelta("6s").as_unit("s").round("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:06')` (i.e., 6s instead of 5s). Example: `pd.Timedelta("4s").as_unit("s").ceil("2500ms")` returned `Timedelta('0 days 00:00:04')`, which is not a multiple of the requested `freq` at all.

Correct behavior is to classify `freq` against one unit of the target resolution: (1) if `freq` is a whole multiple of the unit, round normally; (2) if `freq` divides one unit evenly, it is a no-op; otherwise raise `ValueError` using the message already raised in `core/arrays/_ranges.py` for this exact situation (including `freq="2500ms"` on second-resolution data).
